utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Naletilic and Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Before we have the witness, there are several matters I would like to say at this moment. The first one is that we have to finish the testimony of this witness today because we have already kept him here for almost a week, and I believe that this is the last witness from the Prosecution's case. So there will be some procedural matters that both parties would like to address to the Chamber. Secondly, that this Trial Chamber has been seized of some suggestions of the Court recess filed by the Defence counsel. We are now in no position to make decisions on these issues, but one point I would like to remind the Defence counsel is that you asked 20 days for filing your motion for acquittal after the closure of the Prosecution's case. We looked into the Rules, that is the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of this Tribunal. It is said only seven days, which means only a week for you to file this motion. We believe that we have to abide by that Rule. And by the way, if I could, I'll remind the Defence counsel that we hope in your motion you could specify your request, which is count by count rather than to submit an overall rejection. Thirdly, we understand that the Defence counsel asked for a Status Conference. During the proceedings of this case, and now it might be the right time to hold it, sometime tomorrow or next week. I would like to hear the initial response from Defence counsel. Which time will be more suitable for them? Because we have to make the necessary arrangement for the courtroom for the interpretations as well as for the support. Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours, and thank you for giving me this opportunity. I shall be very brief. Yesterday we had a very long and I believe a very satisfactory, mutually satisfactory meeting. We managed to agree on certain matters, and thus we also agreed on the Status Conference and our joint suggestions - I hope my learned friends will confirm this - we all need some time to prepare for it, and we agreed that it would be best to have it on Wednesday next week. It is a Status Conference that we accord major importance to. Because these suggestions that we indicated in our motion with regard to their recess and the Defence case, they all need to be explained very thoroughly to the Chamber, and we want to prepare for it properly. And as we agreed with our learned friends, our joint proposal is that the Status Conference be held next Wednesday. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Mr. Krsnik was quite right. I should also like to add that for tomorrow we have a meeting with Mr. Fourmy, so that tomorrow we shall have a busy day, and these Defence will be very happy to have the Status Conference on Wednesday, and we shall be preparing also our oral -- the oral reasoning of what we have already indicated in our written motion. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any response from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, what counsel said is correct. We met yesterday and had proposed that all things being considered, that next Wednesday would be a time to frankly allow everyone to catch their breath a bit, not knowing exactly how the end of this week would come about, and then be prepared hopefully to have a helpful Status Conference next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So we will have the Status Conference next Wednesday. As for the specific timing and the location, we believe that Madam Registrar will make the proper arrangement and inform us in time. Mr. Usher, would you please call in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Par. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Par: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Sir Martin. I was corrected when I addressed you as Sir Garrod. The correct address is Sir Martin, so that I will do so as of this moment. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. I just said that yesterday in my language, I said that I was addressing you incorrectly and that the proper address is Sir Martin. So this is why I emphasise it. Let me remind you of where we broke yesterday. We started discussing the cause for the conflict between the Muslims and Croats in Mostar in 1993, and today I should like to look at some factors which influenced this conflict and perhaps touch upon the nature of that conflict, that is, the international armed conflict in that area. I believe that the last subject we broached yesterday was the Vance-Owen Plan, so let me ask you some questions about that today. As far as I could gather from your testimony, the Vance-Owen Plan which was a plan for the peaceful solution in Bosnia-Herzegovina, adopted, in early 1993, and that plan, as you yourself said, was in a way an introduction into the Croat-Muslim conflict. It was a plan, and you pointed out that it was not favourable to the Muslims but that the Croats misinterpreted it and tried to implement it. Would that be the correct interpretation of your testimony? Was that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I am not an expert on the Vance-Owen Plan which was more or less, as I said, moribund by the time I arrived in Bosnia, but that is more or less my understanding of how things developed, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I should like to ask you a few short questions to go back a little and try to clarify: Why was the Vance-Owen Plan adopted at that particular time and why was it necessary at all. And in order to arrive at some answer, I will ask you a couple of short questions and you will tell me whether you agree with me or not. So my objective is to establish the foundation, what -- underpin that plan and how it came about. Your explanation is that the war in Mostar between Muslims and Croats was the war about the territories. So my question is: Up to 1993, before 1993, did Republika Srpska exist already as a territorial entity controlled by Bosnian Serbs, and whether during that time, that is, until 1993, did Serbs already accomplish the goals that they were pursuing in Bosnia through Republika Srpska? I have no reason to pursue any further objectives. Would you agree that that was the actual state of affairs in Bosnia in the beginning of -- at the beginning of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Before the war in Bosnia, of course, there was no such thing as Republika Srpska, but by the summer of 1992, the Serbs controlled roughly 70 per cent of the territory of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, that was the Serb position. Would you agree when I say that at the same time, that is, until 1993, the Croats had already more or less accomplished what they had wanted to accomplish, defended the territories as much as they could, they had lost the Sava valley, Jajce, but nevertheless they had taken and were controlling a territory which ensured their survival in Bosnia-Herzegovina? Would you agree that again that was the state of affairs as far as the Croats were concerned and that they also had no further reason for waging a war in that territory at that time, that is, again, early 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they had certainly repulsed the Serb aggression against Mostar, but, of course, as I've said, by now the Serbs were actually controlling 70 per cent of the country. And I don't think that was a very happy situation for either the Croats or the Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll come back to the Bosniaks. But what about the Croats? Was it a position which ensured for them survival in a certain way so that they had no further motivation to prolong the war? Were they perhaps slightly worse off than the Serbs but yet well enough to stay in that area, that is, that there was no longer a reason for them to wage any further war? That is my question.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course, they were certainly not happy with the situation at all, and they had lost territory to the Serbs, and of course by April, May 1993 the fighting between the Croats and the Bosniaks started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. We'll come to May 1993 later. I'm talking about everything that happened earlier, that is, prior to the Vance-Owen Plan. So we know what the Serb situation was, we know what the Croat situation was. Now, would you agree that at that same time, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina actually was in such a situation which could make them unhappy because they had at least territory that they could control in view of the size of their population. So in early 1993 they were faced with a major problem because they had a very small territory and very many people in relation to the territory. So wasn't there the weakest position and didn't they have a reason at that time to look for new territories? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly the Bosniak army wished to regain the territory, in particular, that they had lost to the Serbs. Yes. I mentioned that yesterday. In particular, we're talking about Zvornik, the upper regions of the Drina, Sanski Most, Prijedor, Sava, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in other words, what are we talking about? We're trying to establish what is it that happened before the Vance-Owen Plan. And could we then say that at that time, early 1993, was a relatively calm, a stable period of time as far as the situation on the ground was concerned, that the position had already been more or less defined, and that people's concern -- were more or less interested in freezing that particular situation? In other words, wasn't that a moment when it became quite possible or when it became quite feasible to -- when long-time peace became quite feasible? Could that be the reason behind the Vance-Owen Plan?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, clearly the occupation of 70 per cent of the territory of Bosnia was totally unacceptable, and therefore the Vance-Owen Plan was one of the first major initiatives to try and bring a long-term agreed settlement, agreed by all sides, for the future of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So these were more or less the conditions when a plan of a kind could be drawn up because there were no actual belligerences going on. Everybody was holding his own positions. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I certainly wouldn't call it a stable position at all, at all. What the Vance-Owen Plan was attempting to do was to try and bring a long-term, stable situation in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. But now let us look at how Vance-Owen, international diplomats, international mediators what idea did they come up with so as to introduce a stable and long-term peace in Bosnia. Didn't the Vance-Owen Plan recognise the factual situation on the ground achieved by the force of arms and ethnic cleansing? And on the basis of that split Bosnia into provinces? Wasn't that the basis of the Vance-Owen Plan? The situation is such as it is, and we shall call then these areas provinces, but as a matter of fact the status quo would be preserved. Was that the idea that underpinned the Vance-Owen Plan?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, except for the fact that it required the Serbs to withdraw from many of the areas which they then controlled, into a much smaller area, a much smaller area than the 70 per cent. And as you say, the plan was to split Bosnia into ten provinces. Some had a Croat majority, some had a Muslim majority, some had a Serb majority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, then, does the Vance-Owen Plan mean relinquishing the idea of a multi-ethnic, unified Bosnia, and is the Vance-Owen Plan the basis for the partitioning of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Is that the basis for the partition of Bosnia-Herzegovina adopted by the international community, perhaps in good faith?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Quite the reverse. The aim of the Vance-Owen Plan was to ensure that we had retained a unified Bosnia and Herzegovina. It's now split into cantons. Vance-Owen were going to split it into provinces, some with different majorities, but all on a multi-ethnic basis. Not pure provinces, not pure Serb provinces or pure Bosniak or pure Croat provinces but multi-ethnic provinces but with a majority of one of the nationalities. But it was intended to keep -- to ensure that thereby Bosnia was retained as a unitary state.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. So formally speaking, we can say that this plan is a plan about the unified Bosnia, that it pursues the preservation of that unified Bosnia, its own provinces, such and such. We won't call them a Serb, Croat or Muslim, but in substance, the situation on the ground is blood. One knows what that means on the ground, and that is what the war which erupted then showed. It brought to light the substance of this plan, and what did everybody do? They all took up arms. Now, my question to you is: Could one of the factors behind the war in Mostar be the Vance-Owen Plan which showed those people down there that Bosnia was being partitioned?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think so, because, as I say, the intention throughout was that there may be majority provinces, but multi-ethnic provinces and Bosnia as a unitary state. And of course, the Croats, as I said, were the first to accept it, but I don't think they really examined the small print carefully enough, reading that they were multi-ethnic provinces and the provinces would be governed by multi-ethnic government based on the proportions of the 1991 census.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What Croats, Sir Martin? What Croats? Do you mean the political leadership or do you mean the populous, the Croats? People there, what were they to read? They heard what was happening. They saw who was getting what promised. Did they understand the Vance-Owen Plan precisely in the manner in which I'm telling you? Perhaps they couldn't read the small print. They took it to mean the partitioning of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I'm not talking about the politicians; I'm talking about the grass roots, about the rank and file people on all three sides, that they understood that the Vance-Owen Plan meant splitting up, meant partitioning?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if the grass roots did not understand the situation, that must -- the blame must be put squarely at the feet of their own leadership. It was up to the political leaders of all three sides to explain to their people exactly what the plan meant before they accepted it or rejected it. But it's no good saying that the people on the ground didn't understand. Why didn't the politicians, political leaders, explain to them what it meant?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, we may come back to this particular subject, the politicians, so as not to lose the thread right now. Why am I pressing this point, namely, that the Vance-Owen Plan is based on the idea of Bosnia's partitioning? Because during your testimony, you said, among other things, that anyway, it was a Croat idea as opposed to some kind of a Muslim idea about multi-ethnic nature and so on and so forth. But what I'm saying now is that if we really look at the substance of this idea about the partitioning of Bosnia, could we agree that this idea came from the Serbian aggressor against Bosnia-Herzegovina, who, in a manner, received support for the partitioning of Bosnia through the Vance-Owen Plan? So is the partitioning of Bosnia the idea with which the Serbian aggressor came up and was then indirectly endorsed by the views of the International Community? Nobody in Mostar had to come up with this idea, because this was a process under way and nobody could stop it. Would you agree that this idea was born in the minds of the Serbian aggressor?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that the Serb aggressor had already, de facto already occupied 70 per cent of the land. This was a plan to take back a lot of the territory that had been occupied by the Serbs, and Karadzic certainly did not, he was not in favour of the Vance-Owen Plan, because it would mean him having to give up a lot of the territory which was then actually controlled de facto by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I am trying to get at here is to say that the idea about the partitioning of Bosnia did not come from Croats, that it came -- that it was born by itself but from a process. Let us look at some concrete facts. For instance, would you agree that the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as an independent state, gained its independence after following a referendum in which the Croats and the Muslims said, "We want an independent state"?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree that without that Croat voice, without that Croat vote, without their desire to have this united state, that state would not have come into being then, or rather, now?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I can remember, the figures of the referendum I think were something like 98 per cent in favour, but that was excluding the Serbs, of course, who did not -- boycotted the referendum.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, quite. We'll come to that. So the Croat idea is very clearly expressed at that time. What kind of Bosnia do they want? They want a joint state with Muslims, an integral state, very clearly stated. Now, at that time, it was a common fact what you have just said, the Serbs say no, they don't want that and they start a war. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean, the war started, initiated by the Serbs long before, of course, the Vance-Owen Plan was even thought of, so I agree. And Serbs were after their -- Milosevic was after his Greater Serbia. I think that's accepted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we agree that the partition of Bosnia-Herzegovina is no longer theoretical. It is introduced through shelling, ethnic cleansing, in a war waged by the Serbs against the Croats and Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at that point in time, can we agree that the Serbs are strong, that they enjoyed the support of the former Yugoslav People's Army, they have weapons, tanks, air force, logistics, and that they have an absolute military advantage over the Croats and Muslims, who had no army, no weapons, no defence concept. Was that the military situation at the time?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Serbs, of course, had all the ammunitions and hardware, the tanks, the guns, and so on, of the JNA, the Serb National Army. Correct. That is so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then, Sir Martin, didn't the Security Council, the UN Security Council, in its well-known resolution 713, didn't it say, "We prohibit the delivery of weapons to Croats and Muslims and all the other Yugoslavian republics. We impose an embargo on arms. You may not be armed." Is that an accurate statement?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not "you may not be armed," it was imposing an arms embargo preventing countries to supply arms to those Serbia, Croatia, and the Bosniaks. Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir Martin, it is -- so the word "resolution" always sounds so nice and they say "We prohibit the supply of weapons, the sale of weapons." But what it means is you allow us to be slain, because what it means, its substance means that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean, I think we could spend a long, long time, a very interesting discussion, on the arms embargo. All I would say is that of course it affected the Croats and the Bosniaks far worse than it did the Serbs, who had a two-year supply, could fight a war for two years without any resupply. But of course then slowly Croatia very commendably started to get in weapons from outside and indeed so did the Bosniaks. Not heavy weapons, but weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir Martin, we are about to come to that, international conflict, international cooperation, and so on and so forth, but we can agree the Muslims, the Croats do not have any weapons, they don't have any assistance from the International Community; that is, it is not going to stop the intervention and therefore they have to turn to somebody for help. Was that how it was at the time?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not say they had no weapons. They were affected by the arms embargo, of course, but they did have weapons, less than, of course, the Serbs, and they did not have the heavy weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we then agree that they simply have to turn for help? The Croats to their Croatian brethren and the Muslims to their Muslim brethren, as it was said? Wouldn't it be the logical evolution that they turn to those -- to other sides for help?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course they're going to try and get weapons from where they can, because they were in the middle of a war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we now, in regard of this situation where they looked for help -- at Croatia for help, how it looked from the Croatian vantage point, what were their reactions? At that time the Republic of Croatia, the Croatian state, was assisting the HVO, the Territorial Defence, that is, the Muslims. Did they assist, logistically speaking, to these factions? For instance, did they allow the Territorial Defence, which is the precursor of the ABiH, to form their units in their territory and to train those units there?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but of course at that time the Muslims and the Croats were fighting together before they started fighting against each other. But until then, they had been fighting in the same formations against the Serbs, and of course indeed up in Tuzla, they still continued to do that throughout, in Tuco.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but is there now an international aggression against the Serbs? If Croatia is giving arms to the Muslim Bosniaks to fight the Serbs, is that the Croatian aggression against the Serbs in Bosnia? In other words, is it considered that if the Croatian state is assisting the Muslims, is that considered all right if it is assisting the Croats, then it is an international armed conflict? And we have to bear in mind that the Muslims and the Croats are both fighting the Serbs, the third party within Bosnia. So my question is: Did the International Community view in the same way, by the same standard, the assistance that was provided to the Muslims and to the Croats from Croatia, for instance?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the International Community must have realised that of course there were weapons coming across from Croatia into Bosnia which were supplying both -- for which the HVO and the ABiH were benefitted, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one more thing regarding this assistance. At that time the Muslims were getting some assistance from the Middle East countries and then the Mujahedin arrived, which I'm not going to mention again. And Croatia helped them go to Bosnia to fight with their Muslim brethren. In other words, the Muslim assistance that came from the Islamic countries, that was going, bound for Bosnia, went through Croatia; in other words, Croatia assisted in this? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I don't know. I never have known exactly the entry point of those Mujahedin into Bosnia. I don't know how they got in, what routes they took.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think we can clarify that easily. On the one side you had Serbia, Montenegro, and the rest of the border is Croatia. Obviously they did not come through Serbia or Montenegro, so I think that only one route was possible. But if you don't know, you don't know?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know for a fact, but what you say sounds sensible, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, there's another interesting point in this situation. When we have Croat citizens, Croatian citizens coming to Bosnia to fight there. We know that at the same time we had a war in Croatia, the Serbs, but now the Serbs from Croatia held certain territories occupied in Croatia, Knin and areas that you are probably familiar with. All these Serbs, let's call them rebels, they are all Croatian citizens. They are citizens of the Republic of Croatia. And they were going to Bosnia with their weapons and fought with their fellow Serbs. And in Bosnia they were constantly fighting for the Serbian cause there, with their tanks and arms and manpower, as volunteers. Is Croatia then responsible, internationally speaking, that their citizens are fighting in this war? Do you distinguish between the role of Croatia -- in other words, is there a distinction between the Serbs from Croatia who went there to fight, or if the Croats from Croatia went to fight? What was -- what part is the aggression and what is not?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would say that the Croatian government was not controlling those Serbs in the Krajina areas. Now, how many they, the Serbs Krajina area had their own problems, but I don't know how many of them moved into Bosnia. It is clear that a lot of the JNA, the Serb regular army, were in Bosnia, but just how many of the Serbs from the Krajinas came into Bosnia, I don't know. But, as I say, I very much doubt whether they were under the control of the Croatian government. Certainly not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would agree with that. And we also don't know whether some Croat -- or Croatian volunteers who went to fight in Herzegovina, whether they were under a control of the Croatian government or whether it was just a call of their families or call of their ancestral lands or something that led them there. But let's try to establish a simple truth that in Bosnia and Herzegovina there were three constituent groups who were fighting each other, all three?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have not objected this afternoon yet at all, but I think the last statement by Mr. Par takes a step too far. He did make clearly a speech that didn't go into a question, nor did he give Sir Martin a chance to respond whether he agreed with him or not. He led up to all these questions about the Croatians going and whether they were volunteers and then there was never a question. And I think -- my apology. I think Sir Martin should have a chance to respond to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Par, besides that objection raised by the Prosecutor, we also have some concerns about the form of your question. We believe that those questions are outside the scope of the indictment, as well as the direct examination. Please concentrate your questions on those events which are related to the indictment, as well as to the direct examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it is our position that one of the key issues in this case is the existence of an international armed conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that this is the question of all questions, or the mother of all questions, as far as my client is concerned. Today I have a competent witness, excellent reputation, and he has been announced by the Prosecution as a witness who will be an expert in the international arms conflict issues. Therefore, I believe that it is my right to put my case to him and to ask for his comments so as to see how this issue of the international armed conflict can be judged and how much light we can shed on it. I will endeavour, in any case, not to go too broadly in my questions, not to go into any speculation, and to allow the witness to express his position as much as possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Ask some specific questions with the proper time frame.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Can I just say something, Mr. Par, that the proposition that you put to this witness, and unfortunately didn't give him an opportunity to respond, which has not been your form so far. I'm sure it was inadvertent - is an interesting one and perhaps it would be good for this witness to respond, and that is your thesis that Croatian volunteers fighting in Bosnia in response to a call to defend their ancestral lands or for whatever motives may equally not have been under the control of Croatia. Now, it would be very interesting, I think, for everybody to hear what Sir Martin has to say in response to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that is not exactly my thesis. The thesis of this Defence is not that only those who were called by their families went there to fight. It was a comment of mine which I myself consider to be a bit of a speculation, and this is why I did not invite this witness to respond to it. And it was to draw a parallel between them and the Serbs who definitely were not under the control of the government. But perhaps I should give Sir Martin an opportunity to answer this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir Martin, you heard what Her Honour had asked, and maybe you can give us your comment on it. Do you distinguish between what the Bosnian Serbs were doing and what the Croats and Serbs from Croatia were doing?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I say, the Serbs from the Krajina areas in Croatia were not under the control of the Croatian government. Now, there may well have been volunteers that have come to fight in Bosnia. There were certainly mercenaries. And I know Mladen Naletilic and his brigade had people of many different nationalities including Germans, English and so on. But what I'm saying is that of course there may well have been volunteers. A lot of them came from, originally from Bosnia, including Gojko Susak, the Defence Minister. But that is slightly different from what I was describing either yesterday or the day before of large regular army formations moving into another country.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe that Sir Martin clarified that point. I'm just going to take you very briefly to this area of different ethnic groups and the international armed conflict and try to establish certain facts. In your evidence, you said that you did not consider that to have been a civil war, if I understood you correctly. My question to you is this: If, in Bosnia, there were three constituent groups or peoples who fought each other, so three people of Bosnia were fighting in Bosnia, they were fighting each other, if this is not a civil war, what else was it? I mean, what characteristics or features do you find that that does not make it a civil war?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I started by speaking my own views. It started as a war of aggression from Serbia. Milosevic, by putting in his paramilitaries, people like Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan and his Tigers and the Bijeljina and then it was followed up by regular forces. So it started as aggression from outside Bosnia. Indeed, throughout the centuries, I think I'm right in saying fighting has never actually started in Bosnia ever; it has always come from outside. This time it came from Serbia. But I would say that eventually, the fighting, some of the fighting, had many of the characteristics of a civil war, particularly in a multi-ethnic city like Mostar. That developed the characteristics of a civil war even though the war started -- was initiated by external aggression.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I absolutely agree with you that the war started by the Serb aggression and then the situation developed into a civil war, that the Croats jumped in and everybody was fighting everyone else. Let us now focus on Mostar a little bit and deal with your monitoring mission and the things that were going on in Mostar. And if we take into account this multi-ethnic Bosnia, you said that you had a number of meetings with Bosniaks, with their military leadership, political leadership, and that they all expressed to you a very clear position that they were for a unified, multi-ethnic Bosnia. My question to you is this: Did you believe them when they said that -- did you believe that what you -- what they were telling you was really their position?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the absence of any alternative, yes, because they were not -- the Serbs were out to get their Republika Srpska. The Croats were anxious to obtain their Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. Bosniaks were not after any specific area. They wanted to retake all the territories which they had lost to the Serbs, and that was throughout Bosnia, not in a portion, not like Republika Srpska, a portion of Bosnia, or the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, but throughout Bosnia. And back to the situation where you had Croats throughout the whole country, Serbs throughout the whole country, and Bosniaks throughout the whole country.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this is a position that they presented to you and that looked acceptable to you. However, did you at the same time see or did you have any information, either from your teams on the field or anywhere else, that in the areas under the control of these same military commanders, that the ethnic cleansing was going on as well, that it was also -- that there were a collection of concentration camps, that it had nothing to do with multi-ethnic proclaimed aims, objectives, and that the reality was completely different? Did you ever notice this discrepancy?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that no side was guiltless, by any means. There were varying degrees of guilt, but never, ever, since I very first went out to Bosnia, have I heard or seen anything which indicated that the Muslims or the Bosniaks wished to divide Bosnia into one, two, three bits, or whatever. There's no concept of how they would divide it if they wished to divide it, and therefore they've always said they did not want to divide it, and therefore I must believe that. Because what portion of Bosnia would they have wanted, had they wanted to divide it? So I don't believe that that is so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. So that means maybe they did not want to partition it. Maybe they wanted to dominate it, they wanted to be a people that would suppress or repress others. You're talking about multi-ethnic character, but the reality in the territory under their control is not giving any signs of their actually nurturing this exotic plant called multi-ethnicity. Perhaps some of -- you're aware that some of the people that you have spoken with are now the accused before this same Tribunal, accused of ethnic cleansing in certain areas around Zenica and elsewhere. So my question to you again is whether the ideas advocated or presented to you by these Bosniak leaders have proven to be something that was not borne out by the reality on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would certainly, as I say, I repeat: There are faults on all sides. And I would like to see Sarajevo a much more multi-ethnic city today than it is at the moment. But if we're talking about division of the country, there is no evidence whatsoever that the Bosniaks wished to divide the country where there's clear evidence that the Serbs did and the Croats wished to have their own third entity. In other words, the Republika Srpska, Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, and whatever is left for the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir Martin, you're prompting me to ask another question now by your answer. If you're talking about the Croats, Bosniaks, Serbs, are you talking about their political leaders? Am I understanding you correctly? You are not talking about common folks, about Bosniak, Croat, or Serb population; you're talking about their leaders. Am I understanding you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Inevitably, inevitably, I think we're talking about political leadership, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, why do I ask you this? As a monitoring mission there, you developed information from them whether they wanted ethnic divisions or not. You did not talk to the common people who basically wanted a Bosnia without any blood-letting. Did you seek to get information from that level or did you basically base your information on your contacts with political leadership of all three factions?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had we had more time, it would have been fascinating to go out into the streets and talk to the man in the street, but frankly, there was not enough time, and we had to rely on the views of the political and military leaders, because those are the ones who are going to shape the future course of events.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. Let us try to move towards the end and move on to another subject which is perhaps slightly easier. Sir Martin, could you please answer me now, as somebody who has military experience, as a General. Will you please answer a couple of short questions that I have in relation to the situation in Mostar in 1993, as a military. 1993, Mostar, the conflict between the Croats and Muslims starts, and now, regardless of who was the one who fired first, what was the situation of military conscripts, of men of military age in Mostar at that moment? Did they have to join HVO units of their own will or would they be called up? Did they have any other option but to become soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course, many of the Muslim men of military age were by now locked up in the Heliodrom, Dretelj, Gabela, and so on, but as far as the remainder is concerned, my understanding is that there was a compulsion on men of military age to serve, on both sides, both in the HVO and in the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's what I'm asking. And you just said it, that is, those who were Croats had to join the army and those who were Muslims, in West Mostar, had to go to Gabela, that is, to prisoners' centres. That is how I understood you. That is how you saw their fate?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said that there had already been a large number of Muslim men of military age detained, but of course those in East Mostar, those that were there of military age were of course required to serve.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's keep to West Mostar. So who takes the decisions? At what level do we have the decision making at the time. Who is it who decides on the mobilisation: You join the army, you go to prison, you go to Heliodrom? At what level are such decisions taken? From what level -- from what echelon do the orders come and which then end up in those developments and those events which are alleged in the indictment? At what level are these decisions made as to what the soldiers' tasks will be?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know, but I can only guess, and I assume that it was the Minister of Defence and the Deputy Minister of Defence in close connection with the other political leaders of the Croats. That's how it would normally work, and I assume that's the way it did, but I have no knowledge of the mechanics of the call-up procedures and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. So now those able-bodied men of military age in West Mostar, Croats are called up and put on the separation line in Mostar, this war is under way, and they are manning that front. Now, my question is: Do they -- they are put on this front line. Can they have any say with regard to some strategic issues happening in Herzegovina or in Mostar or is it that they are assigned to a task with a limited scope?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this point I think we have to say that I think Nuremberg established that following orders is not a defence. I would object to further inquiry in this regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Par, rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Then I will put it in a slightly different way. So that soldier, that foot soldier, a Croat, HVO, a soldier on the Bulevar, he is fighting against an ABiH soldier for months there at that place. Does he have the information, in view of his rank, as a General, what do you think? Does he have any information that would tell him that he is involved in an international armed conflict or is it that he believes that he is involved in a conflict between Aleska Santic Street and Mesa Selimovic Street. Would that be the idea that the soldier has? Does his position there on that front line, does it allow him to have any idea of a broader strategic plan or anything?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object to speculation as to what the individual soldiers knew. I mean, I understand the general principle, but I think we all understand that there's probably different levels of knowledge, but to ask this witness is just pure speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Par, skip this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can do that, but my questions were to learn something from a witness who has -- who is an expert on matters military, who is a General, who knows it and can answer it off the top of his head like this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, does the strategic information ever reach a foot soldier on the front line?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would say that the soldier serving in Aleksa Santic Street would have been solely concerned with Aleksa Santic Street and wondering whether he was going to survive the next 24 hours. I don't think he would be concerned with the Vance-Owen Plan or the wide picture.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And to conclude: The Washington Accords of 1994 are eventually adopted and peace set in in Bosnia, in Mostar, in 1994, thanks to the Washington Accords. Is that an accurate statement?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would it's more accurate to say that -- I wouldn't say peace sets in. I would say a stopping of the fighting, but I would not call it true peace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Quite, and my question was in that direction. Can you tell us, based on your own experience and how you saw it, were Mostar and Bosnia split up then, or are these multi-ethnic cities, that is, states? That is, now, after all that happened, has Mostar become a unified, multi-ethnic city, or is it a partitioned city? Does anyone know the answer to that question? Do you know it? Can you tell us what option has had the upper hand?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would say that in 1990 -- after the Washington Agreement, Mostar was a totally divided city, but the reason why it was totally divided was because the Croat side would not permit any freedom of movement. And we used to be fighting this particular battle every single day, attempting to get freedom of movement from east to west, from west to east. And it was -- as I think I indicated maybe yesterday, the problem that we faced was the hard-line people we were dealing with on the Croat side who did not wish to see a unified Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you for your patience, Sir Martin. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Scott, are you going to do your re-examination, or we break here?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I do have redirect.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Scott

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I do have re-direct, Your Honour. And I'm not suggesting that we lose the time, but it might just as well be that we take an earlier break and start earlier again rather than start one or two questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We might break here. Mr. Usher, would you bring the witness out of the room first. We'll resume at 20 minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, before the witness comes in, a very short question. May I? Your Honours, I must seek an explanation, or perhaps I simply did not understand it right, regarding our submissions for -- our motion for acquittal. We've also studied the Rule 98 bis, which says, in its last sentence, and within seven days of the close of the Prosecutor's case and in any event prior to the presentation of evidence by the Defence pursuant to Rule 85(A), and then Rule 127. We should like to ask for a slightly longer period of time. We are asking it, and we believe we have a strong case to do it. Of course, we were very specific and very concrete in our motion to the Chamber. We presented our view, our position, in very clear terms. If I'm correct, and my learned friend will correct me if I am, but I believe they also agreed that we could have 14 days. But what is important for us is that the countdown starts after the Status Conference, that is, as of Wednesday. You would make us very happy, and of course if our learned friends do not object to it. Because now we have to prepare for the Status Conference, and if we could have seven days as of Wednesday, we would be very happy. But hoping, of course, only that the countdown does not start today. But we shall hear what our learned friends say, or at least that it starts on Monday, that is, to have at least the weekend and the period after Wednesday to write it down as best we can and as best we should. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: As I understand, that the Rule 98 bis said the seven days should be run after the close of the Prosecutor's case. I understand that there are still some documents which will be tendered through this witness. And you also have some time to make a response to those documents. Then the Trial Chamber will make decisions concerning the admission of those documents. And after that, I believe that will be the proper time for the closure of the Prosecutor's case. Then time begins to run. The reason why I mentioned this very issue, to let you know beforehand, so that you could have, you know, proper time to prepare your motion. Maybe right now, but the time will not run from today or from next Monday. I'm quite sure about that. But the Rule said seven days. I think we all have to abide by this Rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, would you please bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I clearly understand the Court's ruling, of course. I just feel as perhaps a matter of honour I should tell the Chamber that when counsel asked me yesterday, I had agreed that -- I had indicated we would agree to a bit longer time. Just so the Court knows and I want to be true to my word to Defence counsel and I had said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But I believe that, you know, your agreement was subject to the rulings of this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I didn't mean to suggest the contrary, at all, Your Honour, but when I make an arrangement or at least offer to make an arrangement with counsel, I want to make sure that I act consistent with that, and I thought I should advise the Chamber that what representations made were correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your information. Any re-examination, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. Re-examined by Mr. Scott:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir Martin, one of the questions that Mr. Par put to you this afternoon was whether there was in fact no reason for the Bosnian Croats to wage war, to continue the war after or as of early 1993. Let me ask you this: Can you tell the Chamber, to your knowledge, did the Bosnian Croat leadership continue to seek after and have as a goal the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna or Republic of Herceg-Bosna throughout 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, and I think I made it clear that in my view, the fighting started because the Croats had misunderstood, deliberately or otherwise, the Vance-Owen Peace Plan provinces and assumed that particularly cantons 8 and 10 -- provinces 8 and 10 were Croat and therefore they wanted to ensure that those were -- and including, that it be right up to Vitez, Busovaca, and so on, and of course, as I said, they wanted Mostar as the capital of their Croatian Republic, Croatian Republic Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And likewise, at least until the time of that the Washington Agreement began to take some substantial form, is it fair to say that they also, the Bosnian Croat leadership also was still seeking some sort of connection, linkage or attachment to the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Washington Agreement had visualised, first of all, the Federation between the Croats and Bosniaks in Bosnia, and then a confederation with Croatia, but that was knocked out in the Dayton Agreement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in terms of questions about fighting that was taking place in the first six months or so of 1993, there are questions about that. Is it correct, sir, or can you confirm to the Chamber that in fact -- my mistake. I'm sorry. Not only early in 1993 but the latter part of 1992, and can you confirm that the HVO attacked Prozor as far back as October 1992?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did they attack Travnik in November 1992?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to remember Travnik. Now, I just cannot quite remember the chain of events in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: It eventually became Bosniak in early 1993, but I can't -- up until then, to the best of my knowledge, it had been mixed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Can you confirm that the HVO initiated fighting in Gornji Vakuf and in Busovaca in January 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is my understanding. That's where --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel and the witness please break between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry. That is my understanding, that the first shots were fired in Gornji Vakuf and Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you also confirm to the Chamber that the HVO launched an initiative or an offensive in the Vitez Kiseljak area in mid-April 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And of course it was in April 1993 that we had the massacre at Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to confirm that one of the topics we've spent a great deal of time talking about this week, can you also confirm again, sir, in your view that it was the HVO who initiated the attack on Mostar on the 9th May 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is certainly my clear understanding, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in terms of the referendum for an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina, can you tell the Chamber what would the result have been if the Croats, the Bosnian Croats, had not supported the referendum?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if they had boycotted the referendum, then no doubt all -- if the Croats had boycotted, then whether it would have been accepted by the International Community as the wishes of the country if only the Bosniaks had voted, I am -- it's difficult to say, but the fact that both the Croats and the Bosniaks took part in the referendum and voted for an independent Bosnia, it was accepted, even though the Serbs had boycotted the referendum.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask my question perhaps slightly differently. If the referendum had not passed, what would the result have been, for both the Croats and the Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I suppose the International Community might not have accepted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Par.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think this is a speculative question. The witness cannot say what would have happened if something had or had not happened. Simply, it is too speculative, and I trust you will not allow this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, it is speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'll move to a different question, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir Martin, let me put a similar question to you this way, perhaps if it assists: By voting for an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina, was that in any way inconsistent as a step on the road to the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was an independent Bosnia as it had been an independent Slovenia and an independent Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, questions going back to Mr. Meek's cross-examination. Fairly early he asked you if -- sorry. He asked you whether it would be unfair to use your interpreter as a source. And Sir Martin, I'd like to clarify that, because sometimes in a military or law enforcement context, the word "source" may have a particular meaning. Now, would you have ever considered, for instance, using an interpreter, one of your interpreters as what someone might call a spy?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly not. We were very conscious that all those interpreters, whether they were Croat or Bosniaks, were always in a very sensitive position, and therefore we were very careful not to undermine their position in any way at all. Inevitably, if one took a Croat interpreter to a Bosniak meeting, she or he would be regarded with suspicion and vice versa. So one had to be very careful indeed, and certainly not use them as, as you say, spies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But is it accurate to say that you did engage in day to day conversation with in your interpreters in which you might learn what was happening in the area?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. When one was travelling from A to B, one would talk. But we were always careful not to engage them in trying to elicit their views on specific, particularly sensitive political or military topics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, as I understand your testimony, there were many Bosnian Croats in Bosnia with Croat citizenship who in fact even voted or at least could have voted in Croatian elections. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is so. In fact, to my knowledge, all the Croats in Bosnia had Croatian passports.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever understand, and can you assist the Chamber, whether in fact some of the very strongest support for the HDZ party in Croatia came from the Herzegovinian Croats?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is so. That is so. And as I've said, there were a number of Herzegovinian members of President Tudjman's government.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just so the record is abundantly clear, Sir Martin, I take it from the discussions about joint Croatian citizenship, are you suggesting that any part of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, by the presence of these dual citizens, somehow belonged to the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not, and to my knowledge, they were not dual citizens. They were citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They were citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina. But somehow they were allocated Croatian passports and were able to vote in the Croatian elections.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the very fact that they could vote in Croatian elections effectively meant that they were constituents, we might call them in a democratic system, they were constituents of the Croatian government in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose you could put it that way, yes, but they were citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned yesterday, when General Roso was -- excuse me. Replaced General Praljak in approximately November 1993.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber, if you know, where had General Roso come from at that time?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where he had -- what particular appointment he just moved from, but I know he had spent many years in the French Foreign Legion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know whether he had held any senior position in the Croatian government prior to taking -- prior to replacing General Praljak?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where General Praljak had come from before becoming Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 8607 to 8614. head of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. His background, funnily enough, his background was in the theatre and directing, and his abiding passion was Shakespeare.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally on that question or that series of questions: Do you know who it was that made the decision, effectively made the decision to dismiss General Praljak?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. I speculated about why he was dismissed, and I've said that it could be a combination of events: The destruction of the old bridge, the Stari Most, the lack of general success that the HVO were having at the time, and the crucial loss of Vares, which took place shortly before he was replaced by Roso. But I don't know who would have made the decision. But I think -- no. It would be speculation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, Mr. Meek asked you if a group of 100 Mujahedin would be able to cause a great deal of damage or trouble. Sir Martin, can the same be said about a brigade or battalion of extreme Croats?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Oh, yes. A small number of determined people can achieve -- can do a lot of damage, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Meek questioned you about something -- some statement or some fact not being in your 1998 witness statement, and you began to say something to the effect that that was not what the statement was about, but I want to give you a further opportunity to clarify what you mean, if you recall that question.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which -- I'm sorry, which one was that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Meek asked you about something -- put it to you that something was not contained in your 1998 witness statement. That Tuta was not mentioned in your statement.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. Indeed. And I think I said because the subject was basically the subject of that particular statement was Central Bosnia and Dario Kordic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You gave some answers mentioning the Catholic church, and I think, sir, lest we receive inquiries from the Vatican, perhaps you should be more specific. Was there some particular component or part or group of the Catholic church that you say opposed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that the Catholic church is not mentioned in the indictment. I don't think that the Catholic church was mentioned here. It is not in the indictment or it's not subject of the indictment. We're not here to try the church. And in any event, I don't think that the witness, whom we all respect here, should not be bothered with these questions. I'm lead counsel here and I felt obliged to get on my feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, it was mentioned in question -- in both cross-examinations both by Mr. Meek and Mr. Par.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We understand that the Catholic church was mentioned. That's quite sure. But we don't know how relevant this issue is to this very case. Is there any point to pursue it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think there is, Your Honour, several things. One is, I think it's really unfair to leave a broad statement on the record like that without clarification, which can only be perhaps viewed by some as inflammatory. Secondly, in the Defence case, I think it will come up and I think it needs to be clarified. This witness is in a position, I believe, to clarify it, and I think he should be given a chance to do so while he is here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm very surprised that my learned friend is speculating, or perhaps he already has some knowledge about what my case is going to be. But something rang a bell. The Croatian press is filled with comments about my Defence and the information that no one should have known, as has been published. I may even seek protection from this kind of obstruction, perhaps at the Status Conference next week, based upon what my learned friend has said. But in any event, we cannot discuss issues and present context here which are not contained in the indictment. I repeat this, and I'm sorry if I'm taking the time to do so, but I'm not sure that I understand what kind of general questions or what kind of speculations may be -- may have anything to do with this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission, Mr. Meek told me that he had asked not a single question about the Catholic church, and because this is a re-examination, I think the question is completely inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we believe that during these proceedings, at least during the direct examination, the witness answered questions concerning the view expressed by the Catholic church, as well as in other witness's testimony. Let me hear what this witness is going to tell us. Then at a later stage we will decide whether it's relevant to this very case or not. Mr. Scott, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir Martin, can you please indicate: When you said -- when you gave the answers previously, can you tell the Chamber whether there was any particular group or portion of the Catholic church in particular that you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. The Catholic church in Mostar, in Mostar. Perhaps I should explain that the -- there's quite a big gap between the Franciscans and Roman Catholic church.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like the witness to be asked where this information comes from, what year he's referring to, because our case is 1993 to early 1994. There is no mention of this within that time frame. This may refer to something that happened in 1995, 1996. Can we get a clarification? Was this information that refers to 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I believe Mr. Scott will clear it up for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. If the witness can be allowed to finish his answer, then I will follow up with the time frame?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was just setting the scene that there was a schism between the Roman Catholic church and the Franciscans. The Franciscans had been in Bosnia since the Eleventh Century and it is the Franciscans who Croats have turned with their problems over the years. The Roman Catholic church I believe was only established at the time of the Austro-Hungarian Empire of some hundred years ago. To be specific, we're talking about early 1994, when we were -- I was trying to arrange meetings with the bishop of Mostar and Mr. Hans Koschnik. I first had a meeting with the vicar general, the bishop's number 2, and after saying that -- telling me that the E.U. Administration in Mostar was going to be thoroughly humiliating for the Croats, it was going to be like the British rule in India. He then launched into a long, long tirade against the Muslims or Bosniaks, including warning of Islamic fundamentalist state. I then had a meeting with the bishop, who is a very hard man. We did not discuss this subject, but I asked him whether he would -- the mufti in East Mostar had asked whether he could meet the bishop. I put this to the bishop that it would be nice if he had a meeting with the mufti. He looked at me coldly and just said, "Don't interfere." I remarked at the time that the support we were going to get from the bishop in Mostar, the reconciliation between two sides I considered to be minimal or maybe zero.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, for the record, is the mufti that you're referring to of Mostar, was that a man named Sead Smajkic?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You indicated and you did clarify toward the end of your cross-examination, I had made this note frankly yesterday, but can you tell us, in terms of the position of the two parties and by that I mean the Croats and the Bosniaks, concerning the status of the city of Mostar, what was the HVO's first position, if you will, during 1993 about what Mostar should be, what kind of city it should be, their first or preferred position, if you will?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: The HVO?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I could refer to the Croat leadership.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croat leadership wanted Mostar as the capital of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, later, did they fall back to a different position, and what was that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the start of the E.U. Administration, it then became apparent that it was not going to be a Croat city, so then they attempted to make two municipalities, in other words, a Bosniak one on the east side, a Croat one on the west side. In other words, dividing Mostar, with the results of the war virtually down the line of the River Neretva.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Essentially, an East Berlin and West Berlin?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Meek, I believe, it may have been Mr. Par, but one of the Defence counsel asked you questions whether the Croats wanted peace. And sir, can you tell us, can you tell the Chamber again, please: Was it the ECMM's assessment that it was the HVO which was on the offensive throughout Central Bosnia and Mostar in the April/May/June 1993 time period?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course the fighting in Central Bosnia by then had become pretty general, with both sides fighting each other. There was a very big difference. Up in the north, in Tuzla, the Croats and the Bosniaks were fighting together against the Serbs; in Central Bosnia they were fighting each other; and in the south, we had the fighting in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell the Chamber whether the balance or whether the military situation had shifted by the late summer of 1993, I mean, in relation to the HVO and the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation in -- I reckon by towards the end of the year, the balance was shifting against the Croats, particularly in Central Bosnia. In Mostar, the line did not change, although East Mostar continued to be progressively further destroyed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in answer to the question -- Defence counsel's question when you said the Croats wanted peace, was that at a time when they had become at a military disadvantage?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my -- that was my personal assessment. That was about the end of the year early 1994 that they were definitely on the defensive. They had just lost the key town of Vares and they were not having military successes and they saw the ABiH are getting stronger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Sir Martin, as best I can tell, there have been questions seemed to have been raised concerning when you formed some of the assessments you did and the basis for your assessments and perhaps there was some suggestion that in fact some of these views maybe were only formed sometime later and in fact whether these were simplified views. Do you believe you formed simplified views of what was happening in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were up against -- we couldn't wait. We had to produce reports every night, and at the end of the week, a weekly assessment. So these were not views and opinions and facts produced with hindsight. They had to be written on the very day in question to meet the time scale of the various reporting procedures through the RCs to Zagreb and then on to the capitals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Concerning the documents that the Prosecution showed you, from 1993 and 1994, can you just please clarify so the record is clear: Did those reflect assessments or conclusions that you somehow only reached at a much later time, or were those your assessments and observations in 1993 and 1994?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were my assessments and views in 1993 and 1994, at the time that I wrote the reports, which was nearly always on the day of the actual report, although, as I say, at the end of the each week we would produce a weekly assessment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I can just -- I'm only going to take one example, but if I could ask you to turn, please, in the binder to Exhibit 458. Towards the -- not the front, but more toward the front of the binder than toward the back. And of course ..

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've found 458.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you would turn again please to what would be overall, including the cover pages, the fourth page of the document, the list that we looked at the other day, where it says the summary of aims and there were several points attributed to the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, in the interests of time, I had written each of these down in my notes, but I don't see that that's really necessary. I'll just simply pick one. Directing your attention to 3(c), Eventually cleanse provinces 8 and 10 of the Muslims in pursuit of their dream of Herceg-Bosna. Now, as an example, was that in fact your assessment and your observation in 1993 based on your experience on the ground?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would say that was a fair assessment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think finally, you were also asked about the basis of your assessment of Mr. Naletilic, that is, Tuta, which counsel seemed to indicate seemed -- your opinion seemed to be rather negative. Let me ask you this, and I'm going to caution you, in light of some of the cautions that the Court has given me, given us earlier. I don't want you to give any specifics of any other events or conversations or meetings, but just answer this question, please: During the time that you continued serving in or in connection with the Mostar region, from July 1993 to late 1998, did anything happen? And again, don't tell me what or anything, but did anything ever happen or information come to your attention that caused you to form a more favourable assessment of Mr. Naletilic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honour, this question goes well beyond the scope of the present indictment. Now we're wanting to ask the witness questions clear into 1998 and I understand that my learned colleague attempted to be very clever in that question, but it's going way, way past this, and I object, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, let me respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You don't regard this question is in favour of your client?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I regard the question as being -- wanting to bring forth evidence of things that may have happened in 1995, 1996, 1997, and the following years.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, let me respond, please. I am being very careful, in light of the Court's ruling, not to talk about any specific other events or conversations which might have occurred. However, I think this witness was challenged by the Defence as to the basis of the statements that he has made concerning Mr. Naletilic and whether they were ill formed or whether, you know, without basis and without going into any detail I simply asked the witness the question that I did, that based on the totality of his experience in Mostar, did anything ever happen which would have changed his assessment to a more favourable assessment of Mr. Naletilic, and that's my final -- excuse me, counsel. That's my final question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honour, it appears to me that again, for the second time, Mr. Scott has tried to caution the witness before answering, and in the argument not to talk about any specific events or conversations which might have occurred. It's very clear, from Sir Martin's testimony, that he only had one conversation with Mr. Tuta, and that was August 15th, 1993. Only one conversation was ever held. And I'm not going to reiterate my previous objections, because you know what they are, Your Honours. And I'll sit down now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
